title: How Medieval Skeletons, Reductive Genomes and Nine-Banded Armadillos Rewrote the History of Leprosy — Mycobacterium leprae 49%-Pseudogene 336-Day Clock, Triple-Drug MDT Resistance Math, Medieval Urban TB Cross-Immunity (33.3% Threshold) & Nine-Banded Armadillos

teenKit.tldr: By combining medieval bones, bacterial DNA clocks, and wild Texas armadillos, scientists solved a 4,000-year-old medical mystery about how leprosy actually spread and evolved. It turns out this ancient disease has been hiding in plain sight with a uniquely slow, stripped-down genetic code.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how ancient pathogens mutate and interact with our immune systems helps modern medicine track drug resistance and outsmart microscopic killers before they adapt.
keyTakeaways: The bacterium that causes leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) threw away nearly half its functional genes, relying entirely on human cells to survive.
Scientists use a painfully slow 336-day replication clock and ancient DNA extracted from medieval Danish churchyards to map the exact evolutionary history of the disease.
Surprisingly, nine-banded armadillos in the American South are natural carriers of the bacteria, acting as an unexpected living archive for researchers.

vocab.meaning: The study of ancient diseases and medical conditions by examining old bones, teeth, and mummified tissues.
An organism's DNA that has shrunk over time as it deleted unneeded genes, becoming totally dependent on a host.
A damaged or inactive gene that used to do a job in an ancestor's DNA but has mutated and stopped working.
When exposure to one disease (like tuberculosis) accidentally trains your immune system to fight off a totally different but related threat.

quiz.question: What surprising thing did the leprosy bacterium do to its own DNA over evolutionary time?
options: It mutated to grow twice as fast as regular bacteria
It deliberately deleted almost half of its own genes and stopped working independently
It swapped DNA with modern viruses to create new symptoms
It locked its entire genetic code in a permanent mineral crystal
quiz.explanation: The bacterium went through a reductive evolution phase, throwing away nearly half its source code because it freeloads off human cells.

quiz.question: Which unexpected animal in North America plays a major role in modern leprosy research?
quiz.explanation: Nine-banded armadillos are natural carriers of the leprosy bacterium, providing scientists with living samples to study.

quiz.question: What role do medieval skeletons play in solving this 4,000-year-old medical cold case?
options: They carry preserved ancient bacterial DNA that lets scientists track how the disease mutated and traveled across centuries.
They show bite marks from armadillos that lived in medieval Europe.
They prove that medieval people invented the first multi-drug antibiotics.
They contain written medical journals detailing exact treatment plans.
quiz.explanation: Ancient DNA extracted from medieval bones acts as a biological time capsule, revealing the historical lineage and spread of the pathogen.
